find: Coarse-grained rocks have crystals large enough to see with the naked eye (generally above 1 mm). Fine-grained rocks have crystals too small to see individually without a hand lens.
replace: Coarse-grained rocks have crystals larger than 3 mm, easily seen with the naked eye. Fine-grained rocks have crystals smaller than 1 mm, too small to see individually without a hand lens.
note: F1: the spec sets the igneous boundaries at coarse >3 mm and fine <1 mm; 1 mm for coarse deletes the medium band.
F2: dolerite is basic (45-52% silica), the medium-grained equivalent of basalt and gabbro, not intermediate in composition.

find: Examiner reports consistently note that students lose marks by using rock names not on the specification.
replace: Students often lose marks by using rock names that are not on the specification.
note: F3: removes an invented examiner-report source; keeps the advice.

find: Under plane-polarised light, different minerals show different colours and extinction angles.
replace: Under the microscope, different minerals show different colours, shapes and cleavage patterns.
note: F4: extinction angles are seen under crossed polars, not plane-polarised light.

find: look for crystal shape (angular crystals = fast cooling; well-formed euhedral crystals = slow cooling), relative crystal sizes
replace: look for crystal shape (well-formed crystals grew early with space around them; irregular shapes grew last and filled the gaps), relative crystal sizes
note: F5: crystal shape records growth order and available space, not cooling rate; the old rule was backwards.

find: Writing “hornfels” or “anorthite” when identifying a hand specimen will score nothing — use only the names listed on your data sheet.
replace: Hornfels is a rock, not a mineral, and anorthite is not on the data sheet. Name minerals using only the list on your data sheet.
note: F6: hornfels is a rock, so it is a category error in a mineral-naming list; also drops an invented mark-scheme certainty.

find: Never use colour alone as your sole evidence — examiners will not credit it without supporting properties.
replace: Never use colour alone as your only evidence — back it up with hardness, streak, cleavage or the acid test.
note: F7: removes a fabricated claim about examiner behaviour.

find: Clay minerals in a mudstone transform into mica, chlorite and then garnet as temperature and pressure increase toward the conditions of deep regional metamorphism.
replace: Clay minerals in a mudstone transform into chlorite, then mica, then garnet as temperature and pressure increase toward the conditions of deep regional metamorphism.
note: F8: the index-mineral order with rising grade is chlorite, biotite (mica), garnet.

find: lower-temperature fluids at depth produce more soluble minerals including carbonates
replace: the coolest fluids, furthest from the heat source, produce more soluble minerals including carbonates
note: F9: hydrothermal zoning follows distance from the intrusion; fluids get hotter with depth, not cooler.

find: In extended-response questions, three distinct formation mechanisms with a clear mechanism for each will reach the top band.
replace: In extended-response questions, give three distinct formation routes and explain the mechanism behind each one.
note: F10: removes an invented mark-scheme threshold.

find: mixing the two terms is a documented examiner concern
replace: mixing the two terms is a common and costly error
note: F11: removes an invented documented source.

find: Examiner reports flag the confusion between porosity and permeability as one of the highest-frequency errors in this unit.
replace: Confusing porosity with permeability is one of the most common errors in this unit.
note: F12: removes an invented examiner-report source and frequency statistic.

find: formed by density settling from a turbidite current.">Graded bedding</dfn>
replace: formed by density settling from a turbidity current.">Graded bedding</dfn>
note: F13: the flow is a turbidity current.

find: It forms when a <dfn class="term" data-def="A submarine density current carrying a mixture of sediment and water that flows rapidly down a continental slope, depositing a graded bed.">turbidite</dfn> current — an underwater avalanche of sediment — flows down the continental slope.
replace: It forms when a turbidity current — an underwater avalanche of sediment — flows down the continental slope, dropping its load as a graded bed called a <dfn class="term" data-def="A graded bed of sediment dropped on the deep sea floor by a turbidity current.">turbidite</dfn>.
note: F13: a turbidite is the deposit, not the current; the spec lists turbidites as deep-marine rocks.

find: indicates a turbidite current in a deep-marine setting
replace: indicates a turbidity current in a deep-marine setting
note: F13: the flow is a turbidity current.

expect: The sediment was deposited by a turbidite current
value: The sediment was deposited by a turbidity current
note: F13: distractor uses the wrong term; keyed answer index 1 is unchanged.

expect: A turbidite current in a deep-sea or slope setting
value: A turbidity current in a deep-sea or slope setting
note: F13: the flow is a turbidity current.

expect: A vertical size gradient within a single bed, with coarsest grains at the base and finest at the top, formed by density settling from a turbidite current.
value: A vertical size gradient within a single bed, with coarsest grains at the base and finest at the top, formed by density settling from a turbidity current.
note: F13: the flow is a turbidity current.

expect: A submarine density current carrying a mixture of sediment and water that flows rapidly down a continental slope, depositing a graded bed.
value: A graded bed of sediment dropped on the deep sea floor by a turbidity current.
note: F13: the glossary defined the rock as if it were the current.

find: The sequence coal — seat earth (fossil soil) — shale — limestone, repeating, is the classic Carboniferous cyclothem.
replace: Read upwards, the repeating sequence limestone — shale — sandstone — seat earth (fossil soil) — coal is the classic Carboniferous cyclothem. The seat earth is the soil the plants grew in, so it always lies below the coal.
note: F14: the sequence was listed in reverse and dropped the sandstone; the seat earth must sit below the coal.

expect: A large, irregular deep intrusion of granite that forms the bulk of the crust is called a _____.
value: A large, irregular deep intrusion of granite, exposed at the surface by erosion, is called a _____.
note: F15: a pluton does not form the bulk of the crust; keyed answer index 3 is unchanged.

find: and older than any dykes or sills they feed
note: F16: a dyke fed by a pluton can freeze before the pluton does, so the added clause is not a safe rule.
